title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 166 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 800–803 (Night 166, continuing directly from nights-165), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 166 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. Shams al-Nahār's slave-girl goes on with her story to the jeweller: she paid the boatman who brought her mistress back, put her to bed, kept everyone away from her, and nursed her until she came round. Then she gives her mistress's own account of the night: the thieves took her and ʿAlī to their hideout, saw through her claim to be a singing-girl, and, softened towards them, fetched the jeweller from his other house; they ferried the three across the river and left them on the bank, where the night watch found them, and Shams al-Nahār talked her way out by naming herself the Caliph's favourite. She has sent the girl to ask after ʿAlī and to give the jeweller money for the goods he lost. The jeweller goes with her, and she tells him to wait for her near his house. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-sittūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth-and-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixty-sixth night,
sentences.n: The heading is built as before: al-sādisa, “the sixth”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-sittūn, “and the sixty”; then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ قَالَتْ لِلْجَوْهَرِيِّ وَقَدِ انْدَهَشْتُ مِنَ الْفَرَحِ بَعْدَ أَنْ قَطَعْتُ الرَّجَاءَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jāriyata qālat li-al-jawhariyyi wa-qadi indahashtu mina al-faraḥi baʿda an qaṭaʿtu al-rajāʾa minhā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the slave-girl said to the jeweller: And (already) I-was-dazed from the joy, after (that) I-had-cut-off the hope of-her.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the slave-girl said to the jeweller, “I was beside myself for joy, when I had given up all hope of her.
sentences.n: The night opens by repeating the last words of the one before, and the slave-girl goes straight on in her own voice: indahashtu and qaṭaʿtu are read as “I”, as they were at the close of the last night and as amaratnī, “she ordered me”, in the next sentence requires. The letters would also allow “she was dazed … she had given up hope”, but the speaker is the girl. wa-qad with the perfect makes a circumstantial clause, “I having been dazed”; qaṭaʿa al-rajāʾa min, “to cut off hope of”, to despair of.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَقَدَّمْتُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا أَمَرَتْنِي أَنْ أَدْفَعَ إِلَى الرَّجُلِ الَّذِي جَاؤَ بِهَا أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā taqaddamtu bayna yadayhā amaratnī an adfaʿa ilā al-rajuli alladhī jāʾa bihā alfa dīnārin
sentences.l: And when I-stepped-forward between her-two-hands, she-ordered-me that I-pay to the man who came with-her a-thousand dinar.
sentences.i: When I came before her, she ordered me to pay the man who had brought her a thousand dinars.
sentences.n: The print has جاو, which is read jāʾa bihā, “came with her”, that is, “brought her”: the hamza is unwritten in the print and the word carries a stray wāw, which is kept and pointed here as the hamza's seat. A plural jāʾū, “who came”, is also thinkable (there were two men in the boat), but the relative alladhī and al-rajul are singular. bayna yadayhā, “between her two hands”, in her presence. amara with an an-clause, “to order (someone) to”; adfaʿa is subjunctive after an. alf dīnār: after alf the counted noun stands in the singular genitive.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَمَلْتُهَا أَنَا وَالْوَصِيفَتَانِ إِلَى أَنْ أَلْقَيْنَاهَا عَلَى فِرَاشِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma ḥamaltuhā anā wa-al-waṣīfatāni ilā an alqaynāhā ʿalā firāshihā
sentences.l: Then I-carried-her, I and the two-maids, until (that) we-laid-her on her-bed.
sentences.i: Then I and the two maids carried her until we had laid her on her bed.
sentences.n: ḥamaltuhā anā wa-al-waṣīfatāni, “I carried her, I and the two maids”: anā restates the “I” of the verb so that the maids can be joined to it, as in the last night. ilā an, “until”, with the perfect for a past event. alqā, Form IV, “to throw, cast”, here simply to lay down.

sentences.t: فَأَقَامَتْ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ عَلَى حَالَةٍ مُكَدَّرَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-aqāmat tilka al-laylata ʿalā ḥālatin mukaddaratin
sentences.l: And she-remained that night in a-state troubled.
sentences.i: She lay all that night in a wretched state.
sentences.n: tilka al-laylata, “that night”, accusative of time, “through that night”. mukaddar, “made turbid, troubled”, of water first and then of a mind or a life; the shadda is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَتْ الصَّبَاحَ مَنَعْتُ أَنَا لِلْجَوَارِى وَالْخَدَمِ مِنَ الدُّخُولِ عَلَيْهَا وَالْوُصُولِ إِلَيْهَا ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥat al-ṣabāḥa manaʿtu anā li-al-jawārī wa-al-khadami mina al-dukhūli ʿalayhā wa-al-wuṣūli ilayhā dhālika al-yawma
sentences.l: And when she-reached-the-morning (in) the morning, I, I-prevented (to) the slave-girls and the servants from the entering upon-her and the reaching to-her that day.
sentences.i: When morning came, I for my part kept the slave-girls and the servants from going in to her or coming near her all that day.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥat al-ṣabāḥa, “she reached the morning”, with al-ṣabāḥa as an accusative of time: a blend of the plain aṣbaḥat and the formula aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “morning came”. The verb is read as “she”, going on from aqāmat, “she lay”, in the sentence before; the anā after manaʿtu then marks the change of subject, “I for my part”. The letters would also allow aṣbaḥtu, “when I reached the morning”. In manaʿtu anā li-al-jawārī, li- marks the object of the verb, which in Classical Arabic would take it directly (manaʿtu al-jawāriya); this use of li- for a direct object is a feature of Middle Arabic, and al-khadam is joined to it in the genitive. al-jawārī is printed with final ى. dukhūl ʿalā, “going in to (someone)”; dhālika al-yawma, “that day”, accusative of time.

sentences.t: وَفِي ثَانِي يَوْمٍ أَفَاقَتْ مِمَّا كَانَ بِهَا فَوَجَدْتُهَا كَأَنَّهَا قَدْ خَرَجَتْ مِنْ مَقْبَرَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-fī thānī yawmin afāqat mimmā kāna bihā fa-wajadtuhā kaʾannahā qad kharajat min maqbaratin
sentences.l: And on the second day she-came-round from what was in-her, and I-found-her as-if-she had come-out from a-graveyard.
sentences.i: On the second day she came round from what had ailed her, and I found her looking as though she had come out of a grave.
sentences.n: thānī yawmin, “the second of days”, the next day. mimmā kāna bihā, “from what was upon her”: bi- marks the one an affliction sits on. kaʾannahā qad kharajat, “as though she had come out”; maqbara is a burial-ground, so she had the look of one risen from the dead. The hamza of كأنها is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَرَشّْتُ عَلَى وَجْهِهَا مَاءَ الْوَرْدِ وَغَيَّرْتُ ثِيَابَهَا وَغَسَّلْتُ يَدَيْهَا وَرِجْلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-rashshtu ʿalā wajhihā māʾa al-wardi wa-ghayyartu thiyābahā wa-ghassaltu yadayhā wa-rijlayhā
sentences.l: And I-sprinkled on her-face the water of the rose, and I-changed her-clothes, and I-washed her-two-hands and her-two-feet.
sentences.i: I sprinkled rosewater on her face, changed her clothes, and washed her hands and feet.
sentences.n: The print has يدبها, a misprint for يديها, corrected here. رشّت is read as “I sprinkled”, the girl doing everything in this sentence: Classical would undo the doubling (rashashtu), but here the doubled letter is kept whole before the ending, as spoken Arabic does (rashsht), and it is pointed that way. Taken by its letters alone, رشّت would be rashshat, “she sprinkled”, Shams al-Nahār tending herself; but every verb around it is the girl's, and she is the one doing the nursing. The shaddas of رشّت, غيّرت and غسّلت are the print's own; ghassala, Form II, “to wash thoroughly”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَزَلْ أُلَاطِفُهَا حَتَّى أَطْعَمْتُهَا شَيْأً مِنَ الطَّعَامِ وَأَسْقَيْتُهَا شَيْأً مِنَ الشَّرَابِ وَهِيَ لَيْسَ لَهَا قَابِلِيَّةٌ فِي شَيْءٍ مِنْ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam azal ulāṭifuhā ḥattā aṭʿamtuhā shayʾan mina al-ṭaʿāmi wa-asqaytuhā shayʾan mina al-sharābi wa-hiya laysa lahā qābiliyyatun fī shayʾin min dhālika
sentences.l: And I-did-not cease I-coax-her until I-fed-her something of the food and I-gave-her-to-drink something of the drink, and she, there-is-not for-her appetite in anything of that.
sentences.i: I kept on coaxing her until I had got her to eat a little food and drink a little, though she had no stomach for any of it.
sentences.n: lam azal with an imperfect, “I did not cease (doing)”, I kept on; the damma, fatḥa, kasra and damma of اُلَاطِفُها are the print's own. lāṭafa, Form III, “to treat kindly, coax”. aṭʿama and asqā, Form IV, “to give to eat” and “to give to drink”. wa-hiya …, “while she …”, a circumstantial clause. laysa stays masculine before the feminine qābiliyya, with lahā between them. qābiliyya, “receptiveness”, a post-Classical abstract from qābil, “accepting”: here appetite, inclination for food. shayʾan is printed شيأ, and شيء keeps the print's own hamza.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا شَمَّتِ الْهَوَاءَ وَتَوَجَّهَتْ إِلَيْهَا الْعَافِيَةُ صِرْتُ أُعَاتِبُهَا وَقُلْتُ لَهَا يَا سَيِّدَتِي انْظُرِي وَارْفُقِي بِنَفْسِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā shammati al-hawāʾa wa-tawajjahat ilayhā al-ʿāfiyatu ṣirtu uʿātibuhā wa-qultu lahā yā sayyidatī unẓurī wa-urfuqī bi-nafsiki
sentences.l: And when she-smelt the air and the well-being turned towards-her, I-began I-reproach-her, and I-said to-her: O my-lady, look and be-gentle with-yourself.
sentences.i: When she had breathed the air again and health began to return to her, I set about chiding her gently, and said to her, ‘My lady, have a care, and be gentle with yourself.
sentences.n: shammati al-hawāʾa, “she smelt the air”, she breathed again, as ʿAlī did in the last night. tawajjahat ilayhā al-ʿāfiya, “well-being turned towards her”, her health began to come back. ṣirtu with an imperfect, “I began to”. ʿātaba, Form III, “to reproach (as a friend does)”, to chide affectionately. unẓurī, “look”, here “take thought, have a care”. rafaqa bi-, “to be gentle with”: bi- marks the one spared. The shaddas of شمّت and توجّهت are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَدْ رَأَيْتِ مَا جَرَى لَنَا وَقَدْ حَصَلَ لَكِ مِنَ الْمَشَقَّةِ مَا فِيهِ الْكِفَايَةُ فَإِنَّكِ قَدْ أَشْرَفْتِ عَلَى الْهَلَاكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qad raʾayti mā jarā lanā wa-qad ḥaṣala laki mina al-mashaqqati mā fīhi al-kifāyatu fa-innaki qad ashrafti ʿalā al-halāki
sentences.l: For (already) you-have-seen what happened to-us, and (already) there-has-come to-you of the hardship what in-it (is) the sufficiency; for you indeed have-been-on-the-verge of the destruction.
sentences.i: You have seen what befell us, and you have had hardship enough; you have been at the very brink of death.’
sentences.n: mā fīhi al-kifāya, “that in which there is sufficiency”, enough and to spare; min al-mashaqqa, “of hardship”, says what the “enough” consists of. ashrafa ʿalā, “to look down upon, be on the verge of”; al-halāk, “perishing”. The kasras of رأيتِ, لكِ and فانكِ, which mark the feminine “you”, are the print's own, as is the hamza of رأيت.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ يَا جَارِيَةَ الْخَيْرِ إِنَّ الْمَوْتَ عِنْدِي أَهْوَنُ مِمَّا جَرَى لِي فَإِنِّي كُنْتُ مَقْتُولَةً لَا مَحَالَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-Allāhi yā jāriyata al-khayri inna al-mawta ʿindī ahwanu mimmā jarā lī fa-innī kuntu maqtūlatan lā maḥālata
sentences.l: And she-said: By God, O girl of the good, indeed the death (is) with-me easier than-what happened to-me; for I was killed-one without escape.
sentences.i: She said, ‘By God, my good girl, death would be easier for me than what has befallen me. For I was a dead woman, beyond all doubt;
sentences.n: Now the girl reports her mistress's own words, and Shams al-Nahār speaks to the end of this passage. yā jāriyata al-khayri, “O girl of goodness”, a kindly address: my good girl. ʿindī, “with me”, in my judgement. ahwanu mimmā, “easier than what”: min after an elative is “than”. kuntu maqtūlatan, “I was one killed”, as good as dead; lā maḥālata, “there is no escape”, inevitably.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّ اللُّصُوصَ لَمَّا خَرَجُوا بِنَا مِنْ بَيْتِ الْجَوْهَرِيِّ سَأَلُونِي وَقَالُوا لِي مَنْ تَكُونِينَ أَنْتِ
sentences.tr: li-anna al-luṣūṣa lammā kharajū binā min bayti al-jawhariyyi saʾalūnī wa-qālū lī man takūnīna anti
sentences.l: Because the thieves, when they-went-out with-us from the house of the jeweller, they-asked-me and they-said to-me: Who are you, you?
sentences.i: for when the thieves had carried us out of the jeweller's house, they questioned me: “Who are you?” they said.
sentences.n: kharajū binā, “they went out with us”: with verbs of going, bi- takes someone along, so “they carried us off”. man takūnīna anti, “who might you be?”: the imperfect of kāna in a question, with the pronoun anti added for stress. The shadda of لمّا and the hamza of سألوني are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ أَنَا جَارِيَةٌ مِنَ الْمُغَنِّيَاتِ فَصَدَّقُونِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu anā jāriyatun mina al-mughanniyāti fa-ṣaddaqūnī
sentences.l: And I-said: I (am) a-slave-girl of the singing-women; and they-believed-me.
sentences.i: I said, “I am one of the singing-girls”, and they believed me.
sentences.n: She hides who she is: a singing-girl (mughanniya) was a common sight at such gatherings, whereas the Caliph's favourite could not be. ṣaddaqa, Form II, “to believe (someone)”, takes the person directly; the shadda is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَأَلُوا عَلِيَّ بْنَ بَكَّارٍ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ وَقَالُوا لَهُ مَنْ تَكُونُ أَنْتَ وَمَا شَأْنُكَ فَقَالَ أَنَا مِنْ عَوَامِّ النَّاسِ
sentences.tr: thumma saʾalū ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin ʿan nafsihi wa-qālū lahu man takūnu anta wa-mā shaʾnuka fa-qāla anā min ʿawāmmi al-nāsi
sentences.l: Then they-asked ʿAlī ibn Bakkār about himself, and they-said to-him: Who are you, you, and what (is) your-affair? And he-said: I (am) of the common-folk of the people.
sentences.i: Then they asked ʿAlī ibn Bakkār about himself: “Who are you, and what is your business?” He said, “I am one of the common people.”
sentences.n: saʾala … ʿan, “to ask (someone) about”: the person asked is the direct object, the subject of the question takes ʿan. ʿawāmm al-nās, “the commons of the people”, ordinary folk, as against the khāṣṣa, the great and well-born; ʿAlī too keeps his rank hidden. The hamza of شأنك is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذُونَا وَسِرْنَا مَعَهُمْ إِلَى أَنِ انْتَهَوْا بِنَا إِلَى مَوْضِعِهِمْ وَنَحْنُ نُسْرِعُ مَعَهُمْ فِى السَّيْرِ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْخَوْفِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhūnā wa-sirnā maʿahum ilā an intahaw binā ilā mawḍiʿihim wa-naḥnu nusriʿu maʿahum fī al-sayri min shiddati al-khawfi
sentences.l: And they-took-us, and we-went with-them until (that) they-came-to-the-end with-us at their-place, and we (were) hurrying with-them in the going from the intensity of the fear.
sentences.i: So they took us along, and we went with them until they brought us to their lair, hurrying along with them in the extremity of our fear.
sentences.n: intahaw binā ilā, “they ended up with us at”, brought us to; bi- again takes the captives along. wa-naḥnu nusriʿu, “we hurrying”, a circumstantial clause. min shiddati al-khawfi, “from the intensity of fear”: min gives the cause. فى is printed with final ى.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَقَرُّوا بِنَا فِي أَمَاكِنِهِمْ تَأَمَّلُونِي وَنَظَرُوا مَا عَلَيَّ مِنَ الْمَلْبُوسِ وَالْعُقُودِ وَالْجَوَاهِرِ فَأَنْكَرُوا أَمْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istaqarrū binā fī amākinihim taʾammalūnī wa-naẓarū mā ʿalayya mina al-malbūsi wa-al-ʿuqūdi wa-al-jawāhiri fa-ankarū amrī
sentences.l: And when they-settled with-us in their-places, they-looked-closely-at-me and they-looked-at what (was) on-me of the clothing and the necklaces and the jewels, and they-found-strange my-case.
sentences.i: When they had us settled in their quarters, they looked me over and saw the clothes I wore, the necklaces and the jewels, and my story no longer rang true to them.
sentences.n: istaqarra bi-, “to settle (somewhere) with”, here the thieves bringing their captives to rest. taʾammala, “to scrutinise”; its hamza is the print's own, as are the shaddas of استقرّوا and عليّ. naẓara here takes its object directly: “they looked at”. mā ʿalayya, “what was on me”, what I was wearing; min introduces what that was. ʿuqūd, plural of ʿiqd, “necklace”. ankara, Form IV, “not to recognise, find suspicious”: they mistrusted what she had told them.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا إِنَّ هَذِهِ الْعُقُودَ لَمْ تَكُنْ لِوَاحِدَةٍ مِنَ الْمُغَنِّيَاتِ فَاصْدُقِينَا وَقُولِي لَنَا الْحَقَّ مَا قَضِيَّتُكِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālū inna hādhihi al-ʿuqūda lam takun li-wāḥidatin mina al-mughanniyāti fa-uṣduqīnā wa-qūlī lanā al-ḥaqqa mā qaḍiyyatuki
sentences.l: And they-said: Indeed these necklaces were-not for one of the singing-women; so tell-us-the-truth and say to-us the truth: what (is) your-case?
sentences.i: They said, “Necklaces like these never belonged to any singing-girl. Tell us honestly, speak the truth to us: what is your story?”
sentences.n: lam takun, “they were not”: a plural of things takes a feminine singular verb. li-wāḥidatin, “for one (woman)”, li- of ownership: no singing-girl owns such jewels. uṣduqīnā, “be truthful with us”, the 2fs imperative of ṣadaqa, which takes the person told directly. qaḍiyya, “case, affair”, the matter to be explained; the kasra of the feminine -ki is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ أَرُدَّ عَلَيْهِمْ جَوَابًا بِشَيْءٍ وَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي الْآنَ يَقْتُلُونَنِي لِأَجْلِ مَا عَلَيَّ مِنَ الْحَلْيِ وَالْحُلَلِ فَلَمْ أَنْطِقْ بِكَلِمَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lam arudda ʿalayhim jawāban bi-shayʾin wa-qultu fī nafsī al-āna yaqtulūnanī li-ajli mā ʿalayya mina al-ḥalyi wa-al-ḥulali fa-lam anṭiq bi-kalimatin
sentences.l: And I-did-not return to-them an-answer with-anything, and I-said in my-soul: Now they-will-kill-me for-the-sake-of what (is) upon-me of the jewellery and the robes; and I-did-not utter a-word.
sentences.i: I gave them no answer at all, and said to myself: now they will kill me for the jewels and fine clothes I have on. So I did not utter a word.
sentences.n: The “I” here is Shams al-Nahār herself: the slave-girl is repeating her mistress's own account. radda ʿalayhi jawāban, “to return someone an answer”; bi-shayʾin after a negative, “with anything at all”. fī nafsī, “in my soul”, to myself. li-ajli, “for the sake of”, because of. mā ʿalayya, “what is upon me”, what I am wearing; al-ḥaly wa-al-ḥulal, “the jewellery and the robes”, a chiming pair. naṭaqa bi-, “to utter”: bi- marks the thing spoken. The shadda of اردّ and of عليّ, the madda of الآن and the hamza of بشيء are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَ الْعَيَّارُونَ إِلَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَقَالُوا لَهُ وَأَنْتَ مَنْ تَكُونُ وَمِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ فَإِنَّ رُؤْيَتَكَ غَيْرُ رُؤْيَةِ الْعَوَامِّ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafata al-ʿayyārūna ilā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-qālū lahu wa-anta man takūnu wa-min ayna anta fa-inna ruʾyataka ghayru ruʾyati al-ʿawāmmi
sentences.l: And the ʿayyārs turned to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and they-said to-him: And you, who are-you, and from where (are) you? For (indeed) your-look (is) other-than the look of the common-folk.
sentences.i: Then the rogues turned to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and said to him, “And you, who are you, and where are you from? For you have not the look of common folk.”
sentences.n: ʿayyār (pl. ʿayyārūn), a rogue or vagabond, one of the street gangs of Baghdad; the tale uses the word alongside luṣūṣ, “thieves”, for the same men. The shadda of العيّارون is printed. iltafata ilā, “to turn (the face) to”. man takūnu, “who might you be?”, kāna in the imperfect in a question. ruʾya, “sight”, here what is seen of a person, his look; the hamza of رؤيتك and رؤية is printed. al-ʿawāmm, “the common people”.

sentences.t: فَسَكَتَ وَصِرْنَا نَكْتُمُ أَمْرَنَا وَنَبْكِي فَحَنَّنَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا قُلُوبَ اللُّصُوصِ
sentences.tr: fa-sakata wa-ṣirnā naktumu amranā wa-nabkī fa-ḥannana Allāhu ʿalaynā qulūba al-luṣūṣi
sentences.l: And he-was-silent, and we-came-to-be hiding our-affair and weeping; and God made-tender toward-us the hearts of the thieves.
sentences.i: But he kept silent, and we went on hiding our secret and weeping; and God softened the thieves' hearts toward us.
sentences.n: ṣirnā with imperfects, “we took to (hiding … weeping)”. ḥannana, Form II of ḥanna, “to make tender”; ʿalaynā, “toward us”, marks those the hearts are softened toward. The vowels of فسَكَتَ and the shadda of فحنّن are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا لَنَا مَنْ يَكُونُ صَاحِبُ الدَّارِ الَّتِي كُنْتُمَا فِيهَا فَقُلْنَا لَهُمْ صَاحِبُهَا فُلَانٌ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū lanā man yakūnu ṣāḥibu al-dāri allatī kuntumā fīhā fa-qulnā lahum ṣāḥibuhā fulānun al-jawhariyyu
sentences.l: And they-said to-us: Who is the owner of the house which you-two-were in-it? And we-said to-them: Its-owner (is) So-and-so the jeweller.
sentences.i: They said to us, “Who is the owner of the house you two were in?” We told them, “Its owner is So-and-so the jeweller.”
sentences.n: kuntumā, “you two were”, dual, to the pair of lovers; allatī … fīhā, “which … in it”, the relative clause takes up “the house” again with fīhā. fulān, “So-and-so”, stands in for a name the teller does not spell out.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمْ أَنَا أَعْرِفُهُ حَقَّ الْمَعْرِفَةِ وَأَعْرِفُ مَكَانَهُ أَنَّهُ سَاكِنٌ فِي دَارِهِ الثَّانِيَةِ وَعَلَيَّ أَنْ آتِيَكُمْ بِهِ فِي تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wāḥidun minhum anā aʿrifuhu ḥaqqa al-maʿrifati wa-aʿrifu makānahu annahu sākinun fī dārihi al-thāniyati wa-ʿalayya an ātiyakum bihi fī tilka al-sāʿati
sentences.l: And one of-them said: I know-him the truth of the knowing, and I-know his-place, that-he (is) dwelling in his-house the second; and upon-me (it is) that I-come-to-you with-him in that hour.
sentences.i: Then one of them said, “I know him well, and I know where he is: he is living in his other house. I will undertake to bring him to you this very hour.”
sentences.n: ḥaqqa al-maʿrifati, “(with) the truth of knowing”, an adverbial accusative: thoroughly. annahu sākinun …, “that he is living …”, spells out makānahu, “his whereabouts”. al-dār al-thāniya, “the second house”: the jeweller has another house besides the one the lovers were taken from. wa-ʿalayya an …, “and it is upon me to …”, I take it on myself. atā bi-, “to come with”, to bring. The shadda of عليّ and the madda of آتيكم are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَاتَّفَقُوا عَلَى أَنْ يَجْعَلُونِي فِي مَوْضِعٍ وَحْدِي وَعَلِيَّ بْنَ بَكَّارٍ فِي مَوْضِعٍ وَحْدَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ittafaqū ʿalā an yajʿalūnī fī mawḍiʿin waḥdī wa-ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin fī mawḍiʿin waḥdahu
sentences.l: And they-agreed upon that they-put-me in a-place alone-me, and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār in a-place alone-him.
sentences.i: And they agreed to put me in a place by myself, and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār in a place by himself.
sentences.n: The print has وانفقوا, a misprint for واتفقوا, corrected here. ittafaqa ʿalā, “to agree on”. yajʿalūnī is subjunctive after an, “that they put me”. ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin is accusative, a second object beside the -nī of yajʿalūnī. waḥdī, waḥdahu, “by myself”, “by himself”, waḥd with the possessive suffix.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا لَنَا اسْتَرِيحَا وَلَا تَخَافَا أَنْ يَنْكَشِفَ خَبَرُكُمَا وَأَنْتُمَا فِي أَمَانٍ مِنَّا
sentences.tr: wa-qālū lanā istarīḥā wa-lā takhāfā an yankashifa khabarukumā wa-antumā fī amānin minnā
sentences.l: And they-said to-us: Rest-you-two, and do-not fear-you-two that your-news be-uncovered; and you-two (are) in safety from-us.
sentences.i: And they said to us, “Rest easy, the pair of you, and have no fear that your story will come out. You are safe from us.”
sentences.n: The verbs are dual, addressed to the two lovers: istarīḥā, “rest”, lā takhāfā, “do not fear”. yankashifa, Form VII of kashafa, “to be uncovered”, come to light. amān, “safety, protection”; amānin minnā, “safety from us”, safe at our hands. The shadda of منّا is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ صَاحِبَهُمْ مَضَى إِلَى الْجَوْهَرِيِّ وَأَتَي بِهِ وَكَشَفَ أَمْرَنَا لَهُمْ وَاجْتَمَعْنَا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna ṣāḥibahum maḍā ilā al-jawhariyyi wa-atā bihi wa-kashafa amranā lahum wa-ijtamaʿnā ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then (indeed) their-companion went to the jeweller and came with-him, and he-uncovered our-affair to-them, and we-gathered upon-him.
sentences.i: Then their comrade went off to the jeweller and brought him back, and he laid our case open to them, and we were together with him again.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”: inna after thumma simply marks the next step in the story. The print spells atā, “he came”, with a dotted ي (واتي) where Classical spelling has ى; atā bi-, “to come with”, to bring. kashafa amranā lahum, “he uncovered our affair to them”: the “he” is most naturally the jeweller, who explained to the thieves who the two were; the thief who fetched him is also possible. ijtamaʿa ʿalā, “to gather upon”, be brought together with.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ رَجُلًا مِنْهُمْ أَحْضَرَلَنَا سُمَيْرِيَّةً فَأَطْلَعُونَا فِيهَا وَعَدَوْا بِنَا إِلَى الْجَانِبِ الثَّانِي وَرَمَوْنَا إِلَى الْبَرِّ وَذَهَبُوا
sentences.tr: thumma inna rajulan minhum aḥḍara lanā sumayriyyatan fa-aṭlaʿūnā fīhā wa-ʿadaw binā ilā al-jānibi al-thānī wa-ramawnā ilā al-barri wa-dhahabū
sentences.l: Then (indeed) a-man of-them fetched-for-us a-sumayriyya, and they-made-us-go-up in-it, and they-crossed with-us to the side the second, and they-threw-us to the land, and they-went.
sentences.i: Then one of them fetched a boat for us, and they put us aboard and took us across to the other bank, and set us down on dry land, and went their way.
sentences.n: The print runs aḥḍara and lanā together (احضرلنا); it is kept as one word. lanā, “for us”. sumayriyya, the small Tigris boat met in the last night; its damma and the fatḥa on the second ي are printed. aṭlaʿa, Form IV of ṭalaʿa, “to make go up”: one “goes up” into a boat, so aṭlaʿūnā fīhā is “they put us aboard it”. ʿadā bi-, “to cross over with”, carry across; al-jānib al-thānī, “the other side”, the far bank. ramawnā ilā al-barr, “they threw us onto the land”, put us ashore without ceremony; the shadda of البرّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَتَتْ خَيَّالَةٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الْعَسَسِ وَقَالُوا لَنَا مَنْ تَكُونُوا
sentences.tr: fa-atat khayyālatun min aṣḥābi al-ʿasasi wa-qālū lanā man takūnū
sentences.l: And there-came horsemen of the men of the night-watch, and they-said to-us: Who are-you?
sentences.i: Then some horsemen of the night watch came up and said to us, “Who are you?”
sentences.n: The print has نكونوا, a misprint for تكونوا, corrected here. khayyāla, “horsemen”, a collective feminine in form, so atat, “(she) came”, and then qālū, “they said”, by the sense. al-ʿasas, the watch that patrols the city by night. man takūnū, “who are you?”: Classical Arabic has the indicative takūnūna; dropping the final -na is a regular Middle Arabic feature.

sentences.t: فَتَكَلَّمْتُ مَعَ الْمُقَدَّمِ عَلَى الْعَسَسِ وَقُلْتُ لَهُ أَنَا شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ مَحْظِيَّةُ الْخَلِيفَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-takallamtu maʿa al-muqaddami ʿalā al-ʿasasi wa-qultu lahu anā Shamsu al-Nahāri maḥẓiyyatu al-khalīfati
sentences.l: And I-spoke with the (one) set-over the night-watch, and I-said to-him: I (am) Shams al-Nahār, the favourite of the Caliph.
sentences.i: So I spoke with the captain of the watch, and said to him, “I am Shams al-Nahār, the Caliph's favourite.
sentences.n: al-muqaddam ʿalā, “the one put forward over”, the officer in command of. maḥẓiyya, “a favourite”, a concubine high in her master's regard. The final damma of فتكلمتُ is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي سَكِرْتُ وَخَرَجْتُ لِبَعْضِ مَعَارِفِي مِنْ نِسَاءِ الْوُزَرَاءِ فَجَاءَنِي الْعَيَّارُونَ وَأَخَذُونِي فَأَوْصَلُونِي إِلَى هَذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-innī sakirtu wa-kharajtu li-baʿḍi maʿārifī min nisāʾi al-wuzarāʾi fa-jāʾanī al-ʿayyārūna wa-akhadhūnī fa-awṣalūnī ilā hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: For I was-drunk, and I-went-out to some of my-acquaintances from the women of the viziers; and the ʿayyārs came-to-me, and they-took-me, and they-brought-me to this place.
sentences.i: I had been drinking, and went out to visit some ladies of my acquaintance among the viziers' wives; and the rogues came upon me and seized me, and brought me to this place.
sentences.n: The print has وحرجت, a misprint for وخرجت, corrected here. fa-innī, “for I …”, opens the account of how she comes to be there. sakirtu, “I was drunk”, is read as printed: it is part of the tale she tells the watch to explain why she is abroad at night, and the letters point to no other word. li-baʿḍi, “to some”, marks those she went out to visit; maʿārif, “acquaintances”. awṣala ilā, “to bring to”. The hamza of نساء, الوزراء and فجاءني is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَوْكُمْ فَرُّوا هَارِبِينَ وَأَنَا قَادِرَةٌ عَلَى مُكَافَأَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾawkum farrū hāribīna wa-anā qādiratun ʿalā mukāfaʾatika
sentences.l: And when they-saw-you(pl.), they-fled fleeing; and I (am) able for rewarding-you.
sentences.i: When they saw you, they took to their heels. And I am well able to reward you.”
sentences.n: raʾawkum, “they saw you”, plural, the whole troop; then mukāfaʾatika, “rewarding you”, singular, to the captain himself. farrū hāribīna, “they fled, running away”: the participle doubles the verb for emphasis. qādira ʿalā, “able to”. The hamza of رأوكم and مكافأتك and the shadda of فرّوا are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مُقَدَّمُ الْخَيَّالَةِ كَلَامِي عَرَفَنِي وَنَزَلَ عَنْ مَرْكُوبِهِ وَأَرْكَبَنِي وَفَعَلَ كَذَلِكَ مَعَ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَالْجَوْهَرِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa muqaddamu al-khayyālati kalāmī ʿarafanī wa-nazala ʿan markūbihi wa-arkabanī wa-faʿala kadhālika maʿa ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-al-jawhariyyi
sentences.l: And when the officer of the horsemen heard my-speech, he-knew-me, and he-got-down from his-mount, and he-made-me-ride, and he-did likewise with ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and the jeweller.
sentences.i: When the captain of the horsemen heard what I said, he knew me. He got down from his horse and set me on it, and did the same for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and the jeweller.
sentences.n: markūb, “a thing ridden”, a mount. arkaba, Form IV of rakiba, “to make ride”, to set on a mount. faʿala kadhālika maʿa, “he did likewise with”.

sentences.t: وَفِي كَبِدِي الْآنَ مِنْ أَجْلِهِمَا لَهِيبُ النَّارِ لَا سِيَّمَا الْجَوْهَرِيِّ رَفِيقِ ابْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-fī kabidī al-āna min ajlihimā lahību al-nāri lā siyyamā al-jawhariyyi rafīqi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: And in my-liver now, on-account-of the-two-of-them, (is) the blaze of the fire, especially the jeweller, the companion of Ibn Bakkār.
sentences.i: And now my heart is ablaze with fire for the two of them, and above all for the jeweller, Ibn Bakkār's friend.
sentences.n: Shams al-Nahār's account of that night ends here, and she turns to what she wants done; the slave-girl is still repeating her words. kabid, “liver”, is in Arabic the seat of the passions, where English says the heart. min ajlihimā, “because of the two of them”. lā siyyamā, “especially”: the noun after it may be genitive, as read here, or nominative. rafīq, “companion, friend”. The madda of الآن is printed.

sentences.t: فَامْضِي إِلَيْهِ وَسَلِّمِي عَلَيْهِ وَاسْتَخْبِرِي مِنْهُ عَلِيَّ بْنَ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-imḍī ilayhi wa-sallimī ʿalayhi wa-istakhbirī minhu ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin
sentences.l: So go-you(f.) to-him, and greet-you(f.) him, and ask-news-you(f.) from-him (of) ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.
sentences.i: So go to him, greet him, and ask him for news of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.’
sentences.n: The imperatives are feminine, imḍī, sallimī, istakhbirī, because Shams al-Nahār is sending the slave-girl. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”. istakhbara, Form X, “to ask for news”: the person asked takes min, and ʿAlī, the one asked about, stands as the direct object.

sentences.t: فَكَلَّمْتُهَا وَلُمْتُهَا عَلَى مَا وَقَعَ مِنْهَا وَحَذَّرْتُهَا وَقُلْتُ لَهَا يَاسَيِّدَتِي خَافِي عَلَى نَفْسِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-kallamtuhā wa-lumtuhā ʿalā mā waqaʿa minhā wa-ḥadhdhartuhā wa-qultu lahā yā sayyidatī khāfī ʿalā nafsiki
sentences.l: And I-spoke-to-her, and I-blamed-her for what happened from-her, and I-warned-her, and I-said to-her: O my-lady, fear for your-self.
sentences.i: So I talked with her, and reproached her for what she had done, and warned her, saying, ‘My lady, have a care for yourself.’
sentences.n: The slave-girl now speaks for herself again. lāma ʿalā, “to blame for”; mā waqaʿa minhā, “what came about from her”, her own doings. khāfa ʿalā, “to fear for”. The print runs yā and sayyidatī together (ياسيدتي).

sentences.t: فَصَاحَتْ عَلَيَّ وَغَضِبَتْ مِنْ كَلَامِي
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāḥat ʿalayya wa-ghaḍibat min kalāmī
sentences.l: And she-shouted at-me, and she-was-angry from my-speech.
sentences.i: But she cried out at me, and was angry at what I said.
sentences.n: ṣāḥa ʿalā, “to shout at”; ghaḍiba min, “to be angry at”. The shadda of عليّ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قُمْتُ مِنْ عِنْدِهَا وَجِئْتُ إِلَيْكَ فَلَمْ أَجِدْكَ وَخَشِيتُ مِنَ الرَّوَاحِ إِلَى ابْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: thumma qumtu min ʿindihā wa-jiʾtu ilayka fa-lam ajidka wa-khashītu mina al-rawāḥi ilā ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: Then I-rose from with-her, and I-came to-you, and I-did-not find-you; and I-feared (from) the going to Ibn Bakkār.
sentences.i: Then I left her and came to you, but did not find you; and I was afraid to go to Ibn Bakkār.
sentences.n: The slave-girl is speaking to the jeweller: “you” is he. qumtu min ʿindihā, “I rose from her presence”, I left her. al-rawāḥ, properly going in the evening, in later Arabic simply “going”; khashiya min, “to be afraid of”. The hamza of جئت is printed.

sentences.t: فَصِرْتُ وَاقِفَةً أَرْتَقِبُكَ حَتَّى أَسْأَلَكَ عَنْهُ وَأَعْلَمَ مَا هُوَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣirtu wāqifatan artaqibuka ḥattā asʾalaka ʿanhu wa-aʿlama mā huwa fīhi
sentences.l: So I-came-to-be standing, watching-for-you, so-that I-may-ask-you about-him and I-may-know what he (is) in-it.
sentences.i: So I have been standing here watching for you, to ask you about him and learn how he fares.
sentences.n: ṣirtu wāqifatan, “I came to be standing”, ṣāra with its predicate in the accusative. irtaqaba, Form VIII, “to watch for, wait for”. ḥattā of purpose takes the subjunctive: asʾalaka, aʿlama. mā huwa fīhi, “what he is in”, his present state. The hamza of اسألك is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ أَنْ تَأْخُذَ مِنِّي شَيْأً مِنَ الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-asʾaluka min faḍlika an taʾkhudha minnī shayʾan mina al-māli
sentences.l: And I-ask-you of your-bounty that you-take from-me something of the money.
sentences.i: And I beg you, of your kindness, to take some money from me.
sentences.n: min faḍlika, “of your bounty”, please. The print spells shayʾan as شيأ, with the hamza on the alif of the accusative, and it is kept; its hamza, and that of فاسألك, is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّكَ لَابُدَّ اسْتَعَرْتَ أَمْتِعَةً مِنْ أَصْحَابِكَ وَضَاعَتْ عَلَيْكَ فَتَحْتَاجُ أَنْ تُعَوِّضَ عَلَى النَّاسِ مَا ذَهَبَ لَهُمْ مِنَ الْأَمْتِعَةِ عِنْدَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-innaka lā budda istaʿarta amtiʿatan min aṣḥābika wa-ḍāʿat ʿalayka fa-taḥtāju an tuʿawwiḍa ʿalā al-nāsi mā dhahaba lahum mina al-amtiʿati ʿindaka
sentences.l: For you, no-escape, borrowed goods from your-friends, and they-were-lost on-you; so you-need that you-make-good to the people what went of-theirs of the goods at-your-place.
sentences.i: For you must surely have borrowed things from your friends, and they have been lost while in your keeping; and you will need to make good to people whatever of their goods went missing at your house.”
sentences.n: lā budda, “there is no escape”, stands here as a bare adverb, “surely, no doubt”, with nothing joined to it, as often in later Arabic; the print sets it as one word (لابد). istaʿāra, Form X, “to borrow”. amtiʿa, plural of matāʿ, “goods, household things”. ḍāʿat ʿalayka, “they were lost on you”: ʿalā marks the one who bears the loss. ʿawwaḍa ʿalā, “to make good to”: Classical Arabic says ʿawwaḍa someone, with a direct object; ʿalā here is Middle Arabic. mā dhahaba lahum, “what went of theirs”, lahum marking the owners.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَقُلْتُ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً سِيرِي
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-qultu samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan sīrī
sentences.l: The jeweller said: And I-said: Hearing and obedience; go-you(f.).
sentences.i: The jeweller said: And I said, “With hearing and obedience. Lead on.”
sentences.n: The jeweller takes up the telling again in his own voice. samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, accusatives of an unspoken verb, “(I give) hearing and obedience”, the formula of ready consent. sīrī, “go (f.)”, lead the way.

sentences.t: وَمَشَيْتُ مَعَهَا إِلَى أَنْ أَتَيْنَا إِلَى قُرْبِ مَحَلِّي فَقَالَتْ لِي قِفْ هُنَا حَتَّى أَعُودَ إِلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-mashaytu maʿahā ilā an ataynā ilā qurbi maḥallī fa-qālat lī qif hunā ḥattā aʿūda ilayka
sentences.l: And I-walked with-her until (that) we-came to (the) nearness of my-place, and she-said to-me: Stand here until I-return to-you.
sentences.i: And I walked with her until we came near my house, and she said to me, “Wait here until I come back to you.”
sentences.n: ilā an, “until”. atā ilā, “to come to”: Classical atā takes its object directly. maḥall, “place of alighting”, one's lodging, house. qif, imperative of waqafa, “stand, stop”. ḥattā aʿūda, “until I return”, subjunctive of a time still to come.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning that overtakes. The print splits the name in two (شهر زاد). al-kalām al-mubāḥ, “the permitted speech”, the talk allowed her until dawn; the rhyme ṣabāḥ / mubāḥ closes every night.
